summaries.summary: Twitter user profiles comprise identity and connectivity attributes, and profile changes may reflect identity choices or indicate broader social movements.
The paper studies Twitter profile changes during India's 2019 general elections, held in 7 phases from 11th April, 2019 to 19th May, 2019, citing Narendra Modi's 49 million followers.

The authors examine #MainBhiChowkidar during #LokSabhaElections2019, launched by BJP after “Chowkidar chor hai,” focusing on display name changes after Narendra Modi added Chowkidar on 17th March 2019.

Figure FIGREF3 compares @narendramodi and @RahulGandhi profiles before, during, and after Lok Sabha Elections in 2019, showing the ruling leader changed profile information while the opposition did not.
The authors aim to understand political discourse through profile attributes on social media and introduce the questions addressed.
Analyzing user-profiles in elections requires distinguishing profile change behavior between political accounts and follower accounts, motivating the first research question.
RQ1 [Comparison] asks how often political accounts and common user accounts change profile information and which profile attributes are changed the most.
Although political inclination can be classified from past tweets and community detection, the authors note this analysis has not been extended in detail to user-profiles.
RQ2 [Political Inclination] asks whether users reveal political inclination on Twitter directly or indirectly using only their user profiles.
Behavior contagion is defined as adopting a behavior after an opinion leader adopts it, motivating analysis of the “Chowkidar” movement and the third research question.
RQ3 [Behavior Contagion] asks whether profile change behavior can be catered to behavior contagion effect where followers adopt an opinion as their opinion leader adopts it.
To characterize people in the chowkidar movement, the authors say major topic patterns must be analyzed, leading to another question.
RQ4 [Topic Modelling] asks what the most discussed topics are amongst users that were part of the Chowkidar campaign.
The authors state that their main contributions are summarized in the following points.
They collect daily and weekly profile snapshots of $1,293$ political handles and over 55 million followers over two months during and after #LokSabhaElections2019, promising data and code.
They analyze political and follower handles for profile changes, showing political handles change profiles more and certain attributes change more frequently with subtle behavioral differences.
They show Twitter users support political parties organically through party name mentions and inorganically through movements like #MainBhiChowkidar, analyzing Chowkidar as contagion behavior.
They perform topic modelling of Chowkidar movement users and show they were most likely Narendra Modi supporters and mostly discussed political topics on Twitter.
Data collection has two stages: manually curating political accounts on Twitter, then using them as a seed set to collect profile information of all followers.
For RQ1, $2,577$ Twitter handles were curated as $\mathbf {U}$, of which $1,293$ verified handles formed $\mathbf {P}$, snapshotted daily from 5th April - 5th June 2019.

Using $\mathbf {P}$ as seed, 600 million followers yielded $55,830,844$ unique users, with 9 weekly snapshots from April 5 - June 5, 2019, and $\mathbf {S}$ containing 49,433,640 accounts present in all snapshots.
The dataset contains daily and weekly snapshots for $\mathbf {S}$ and $\mathbf {P}$, collected via Twitter API with 34 attributes, then pre-processed to remove long-inactive handles.

In $\mathbf {S}$, more than 15 million of 49 million users had no tweets or favourites, leaving 34 million Active users, of which only 5 million tweeted in 2019; the authors use 34 million for analysis.
This section characterizes profile change behavior of political accounts in Set $P$ and follower accounts in Set $S$.
In Set $U$, 54 handles got verified throughout 61 snapshots, and average followers of Set $P$ rose from $3,08,716.84$ to $3,19,881.09$, approximately $3\%$ over 61 days.
The authors consider 5 major profile attributes—username, display name, profile image, location, and description—because these identity elements saliently define users' likes and values.
For $\mathbf {P}$, 974 changes occurred across 5 attributes over 61 snapshots, with profile image most changed, display name second, a 23rd May, 2019 spike, and no username changes.
To characterize follower profile changing behavior, the authors study profile snapshots of all users in set $S$ over 9 snapshots.

Among active accounts, $1,363,499$ users made at least one profile attribute change over 9 snapshots, over $3\%$, with more than $95\%$ making only 1 change, around 275 making more than 20, and about 2 changes on average with standard deviation $1.42$.

Over the same 9 snapshots, $54.9\%$ of $\mathbf {P}$ users made at least one change versus $3\%$ of $\mathbf {S}$, and $\mathbf {P}$ made $75.32\%$ changes on average, 25 times more than $\mathbf {S}$.
INSIGHT 1 states political handles are more likely than their followers to engage in profile changing behavior.
Figure FIGREF15 shows profile image and Location are most changed in set $S$, accounting for nearly $34\%$ and $25\%$, while follower handles often change usernames unlike political handles.

Follower handles use usernames to support a movement or person and later revert; of $79,991$ username changes, $1,711$ users of set ${S}$ went back and forth to the same name with Election related keywords.
INSIGHT 2 states users do not change all profile attributes equally, and political and follower handles focus on different profile attributes.

The authors analyze similarity between current and new display names and usernames in $\mathbf {P}$ and $\mathbf {S}$ using Longest Common Subsequence (LCS), where high average LCS scores indicate less significant changes.

Figure FIGREF18 shows nearly $80\%$ of set $S$ users made more significant Display Name changes than political handles, with unrelated attributes at LCS score < $0.5$ for around $10\%$ of $\mathbf {P}$ and $30\%$ of $\mathbf {S}$.
INSIGHT 3 states political handles make new changes related to previous attribute values, while followers make comparatively less related changes.
This section describes political party name mentions and specific political handle mentions in profile attributes as organic support, then studies #MainBhiChowkidar and associated profile changes.

For Indian National Congress (INC) and Bhartiya Janta Party (BJP), $50,432$ users mentioned “BJP” in descriptions in the first snapshot, approximately $1\%$ of active users, with $2,638$ adding and $1,638$ removing “BJP” later.
The authors observe many users wrote in their description that they are proud to be followed by a famous political handle, with examples in Table TABREF22.
An exhaustive search found $1,164$ instances of such description mentions, supporting with party mention analysis that people display political inclination via profile attributes.
INSIGHT 4 states Twitter users often display political inclinations in their profile attributes itself and are pretty open about it.
@narendramodi added “Chowkidar” after “Chowkidar chor hai,” BJP leaders and ministers followed, and users adopted several Chowkidar variants in an inorganic campaign catalyzed by political leaders.

A regular expression search found $2,60,607$ instances in set $S$ adding Chowkidar variants to display names, comprising 241 unique variants with 225 used fewer than 500 times; $14,409$ added it to description, $12,651$ to username, with union 270,945 and intersection 727.
The authors view profile changes following the Prime Minister's campaign as inorganic behavior contagion, noting opinion diffuses easily from opinion leaders with very high follower counts.

Figure FIGREF18 shows an LCS spike between $0.6$-$0.8$, mostly political handles adding Chowkidar, with $95.7\%$ of users in that region, 373 people in set $P$ adding Chowkidar, 315 in that LCS range, and around $57\%$ of set $S$ users in the region adding Chowkidar.
On 23rd May, Narendra Modi removed Chowkidar and urged others to do the same; most users followed, though some continued adding it, and the majority of set $\mathbf {S}$ removed it too.
INSIGHT 5 states the Chowkidar movement was very widespread and illustrated contagion behavior.
LDA Mallet topic modelling with 10 topics and tSNE shows Chowkidar movement users were mostly BJP or Narendra Modi supporters, including students.
INSIGHT 6 states Chowkidar movement users were mostly Narendra Modi supporters and engaged in political topics.
The Related Work section reviews Twitter profile attribute changes, Social Media movements, contagion behavior adaptation through opinion leaders, and this work's contribution.
Previous studies examine Twitter username changes, reasons for changes, name squatting, and profile attributes representing oneself or social movements.
Studies of Social Media in movements describe participation, expression, Twitter tweet insights, LGBT decriminalization reactions, and Gezi Park username changes.
Alternative for Deutschland(AFD)'s success in German Federal Elections, 2017 is linked to online presence, tweet and retweet networks, communities, information flows, and influential leaders.
Opinion leaders influence online behavior adoption, with their performance affecting contagion and their Twitter activity contributing to political involvement.
The work contributes by investigating profile attribute changes relative to influential leaders and profile information changes during the election in the largest democracy in the world.
The paper studies Twitter profile attributes during #LokSabhaElectios2019 using 1,293 verified political leader's profile, 49,433,640 unique followers, 9 follower snapshots, and 61 Political handles.
Most users made at-most 4 changes, profile image changed most, political handles changed more, and about 80% follower changes related to #LokSabhaElectios2019.

Profile attributes can predict political inclination, party names signal organic support, campaign keywords signal inorganic behavior, and the “Chowkidar movement” showed behavior contagion after @narendramodi.
The analysis may help understand how election movements are perceived and sustained through profile attributes and provides baseline data on election campaigns.
